title: The middle centuries, looking back
tomorrow: a plowboy who knows more Bible than a scholar. who said that?

lines: ONE FLASHLIGHT IN A POWER CUT.
cards: In a power cut, one phone flashlight suddenly matters. Now a window made of broken glass: red, blue and gold pieces held together with strips of lead, set high in a stone wall. All day it looks dull from outside.
Then the sun comes through, and a whole Bible story spills across the floor. Broken pieces, glowing, because the light is behind them.

teach.b: People built windows like that in the middle centuries, and John's Gospel gave them a line: “And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.” Four places it shone.
The cathedrals: stone lifted high, glass that turned sunlight into stories.
Francis of Assisi, who wrote that the sight of lepers once seemed bitter to him, until the Lord led him among them and the bitter turned to sweetness.

The plague: stories tell of people who stayed to nurse the sick and bury the dead. And Julian of Norwich, who, tradition says, prayed in a small room built onto a church, with a window where people came for counsel.
None of them drove the darkness out.
John's line doesn't promise there will be no dark. Some readers hear comprehended as couldn't understand it; others, couldn't overcome it.
Either way, the light keeps shining, the way it did all week: a song in a cave, a river of justice, a party for the lost, a branch that stays, a faithfulness new every morning, a crowd of witnesses.

how: Some Christians light a candle when they pray, at home or in a church, and Francis's song of Brother Sun is still sung and read in churches today.

s: the middle centuries were nothing but darkness
cathedrals, Francis, the plague nurses, Julian: people kept lighting things.
the KJV says the darkness 'comprehended it not' in John 1:5
some hear couldn't understand it; others, couldn't overcome it.
Francis says being among lepers was always easy for him
he wrote that it once seemed bitter, then turned to sweetness.

games.q: a friend's family is having a hard winter: a lost job, a sick parent. she says nothing good can happen until it's over. what does John 1:5 offer, as Christians read it?
o: the dark will lift soon, if she believes hard enough.
light shines in the dark, not only after it's gone.
the dark doesn't matter; ignore it and stay busy.
games.why: John doesn't promise no dark: the light shineth in darkness. Francis, Julian and the plague nurses lit things in the middle of it.

practice: If you have a candle, light it; if not, a lamp or a bright window will do. Watch the light through the sit, and let one dark spot in your week sit beside it, without trying to fix anything.
If you pray, rest on John's line: the light shineth in darkness.

wordCard.voice: The middle centuries. Cathedrals, Francis, the plague and Julian: dark years, and people who kept lighting things anyway.
